newsitem.title: FRANCE: French give tepid welcome to Jospin policies.
newsitem.headline: French give tepid welcome to Jospin policies.

text.p: French people are giving a tepid welcome to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's policies, doubting they will bring a lasting drop in record unemployment, an opinion poll showed on Saturday.
The survey, for France 2 television and the Journal du Dimanche weekly, said 42 percent of people rated Socialist Jospin convincing in his maiden policy speech to parliament on Thursday.
Twenty-nine percent found him unconvincing and the rest gave no opinion. Jospin came to power after the left won an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1.

Seventy-three percent reckoned that the speech matched Jospin's campaign promises, including job creation and shorter working hours. But just 30 percent believed the policies would mean a lasting cut in unemployment of 12.8 percent.

It showed the most popular measure was to teach civic ethics at schools, backed by 94 percent of 967 people questioned on Friday and Saturday. And 86 percent approved his decision to raise the minimum wage by four percent, despite union grumbling it was insufficient.

Least popular was Jospin's suspension of privatisations by the former centre-right coalition, with approval from just 36 percent. Jospin said the government favoured privatisations only if they served the national interest.
A separate IFOP poll showed that Jospin was starting with moderate popularity for a new prime minister, with 47 percent expressing satisfaction and 20 percent dissatisfied.
The survey, for the Journal du Dimanche, showed that his two centre-right predecessors, Alain Juppe and Edouard Balladur, had higher popularity when they took office in 1995 and 1993 respectively.

It also indicated that conservative President Jacques Chirac had grown slightly less unpopular after he gambled disastrously by calling the snap election in the misguided belief that voters would re-elect Juppe's coalition.
Thirty-eight percent of voters were satisfied with Chirac as president against 45 percent dissatisfied. In May, his ratings were 39-52 percent.
